newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan buys fewer imported cars due to tax rise.
newsitem.headline: Japan buys fewer imported cars due to tax rise.

text.p: Sales of imported cars in Japan in April fell for the first time in four months as demand was dampened by a rise in the national sales tax at the beginning of the month, an industry body said Wednesday.
Sales fell a steep 36.8 percent from a year earlier to 20,869 units, the Japan Automobile Importers Association said.
"We expect sales this month and in June will continue to fall. Backlog orders at foreign car dealers are very small now," JAIA vice-chief secretary Kunihiko Ono told Reuters.
Ono attributed the decline in demand to the increase in Japan's consumption tax to 5 percent from 3 percent on April 1 and the weakness of the yen.
Imported car sales rose 12.7 percent to 57,840 units in March, surpassing the previous record for that month of 51,342 marked last year.
"The current level of the yen will hurt sales of imported cars. The yen is unlikely to rise because of the healthy U.S. economy," Ono said.
He said the association expects new models such as Mercedes-Benz's A-class compact car, which will be launched later this year, to help boost imported car sales.
But overall sales in the year to March 1998 are likely to be lower than in 1996/97 because of sharply lower sales of U.S.-made Honda and Toyota cars, Ono said.
Imported vehicle sales in 1996/97 hit a record 437,886 units, up 8.8 percent from the previous year.

"Japanese sales of imported vehicles will fall by some 10 percent this fiscal year mainly because of the weak yen and as Japanese makers import fewer of their overseas-produced cars," Kankaku Research senior analyst Nobuaki Yanachi said.

Honda plans to stop importing its U.S.-made Accord Wagon in a couple of months as it will shift production to Japan from its Ohio plant this summer due to a shrinking U.S. market for the station wagon.
Toyota's Kentucky plant stopped making the Sceptre Wagon in June last year because of poor demand in the United States and introduced the Camry Gracia Wagon in Japan in December as its successor.
Foreign car dealers in Japan such as Chrysler, Ford and Rover have raised prices mainly because of the weak yen.
